subtopic: DAIRY PRODUCTS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF STATEMENT ON STABILIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the minister aware of the fact that concentrated milk manufacturers in their negotiations with producers have quoted from the minister's

Inquiries of the Ministry statement on price stabilization for dairy products, reported in Hansard of April 23, to the effect that "the net result will be to reduce producers' returns by 15 cents per 100 pounds of milk used for manufacturing purposes" as a reason for reducing prices of milk used for manufacturing concentrated products? Can the minister clarify this statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DAIRY PRODUCTS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF STATEMENT ON STABILIZATION
speechtext:
Yes, I would be glad to do so. As a matter of fact I have been informed by several people that one sentence in my statement has been lifted from its context in the paragraph dealing with support prices for butter and skim milk powder and has been quoted as if it also applied to milk used for concentrated products. It was never my intention that such an interpretation should be placed on my statement. In support of this I would point out that I announced support prices for butter, cheese and skim milk powder, but not for any other dairy products.
In the statement I recognized that the subsidy of 25 cents per 100 pounds of milk would not offset the 5 cent reduction in the price for skim milk powder, and that the difference would amount to approximately 15 cents per 100 pounds of milk used for the manufacture of butter and powder. However, my statement was not meant to include other manufactured dairy products such as whole milk powder, concentrated and evaporated milk, which are not under support, since it was assumed that prices paid for milk used in the manufacture of these concentrated products would be determined by negotiation as usual.
Since the statement of April 23 became public knowledge before negotiations were undertaken in Ontario, it is clear that both parties should have had full knowledge of the fact that the government proposed to pay a subsidy of 25 cents per 100 pounds on all milk used in manufacturing.
I need hardly assure the house that I am sorry to learn that my statement has been used in the way indicated by the question which was asked by the hon. member. Consequently I am glad to make this clarification in order that further negotiation or arbitration procedures may be conducted with full knowledge that it was not my intention to deal with the prices of product for which we have no support program.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, May 18, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment and operation of a national energy board and the appointment of its members and staff, to define its duties, to authorize it to exercise certain powers and to provide for other related and incidental matters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his statement last night the minister outlined in some detail the powers that would be exercised by the national energy board and to some extent the type of policy that the government would wish it to follow. The minister stated, as found on page 3767 of Hansard:
We recognize the need for and welcome capital whether domestic or foreign for investment in the energy and associated industries, and we believe such capital, wisely invested, should enjoy a fair and reasonable rate of return. As to what is a fair return, it is not our intention to incorporate any fixed formula in the statute. Rather, our first premise is that returns on successful investment must be sufficient to attract capital for replacement and expansion, and our second premise is that the public interest requires that no pipe line company should exploit its monopoly or quasimonopoly position to secure returns higher than are fair and reasonable.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the stated policy of the government is far removed from what was once the policy of the Conservative party when it formed the opposition. We in the C.C.F. believe that natural monopolies such as gas pipe lines or oil pipe lines crossing interprovincial boundaries should in
National Energy Board the national interest be publicly owned. We support that position not because of any theoretical belief that public ownership in every field is the right way to proceed but because we believe this is a particular example of the kind of utility, the kind of industrial facility, that should be publicly owned. If our natural gas pipe lines were publicly owned, if the trans-Canada gas pipe line were publicly owned, we feel that this would assist in providing energy sources for Canadian industry at the lowest possible price. At a time when the house is giving serious consideration to the whole question of inflation, to the whole question of our high cost economy-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would hon. members please talk a little more quietly. It is rather difficult for the Chair to hear the member who has the floor.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I was saying that at a time when inflation is very much in the minds of members of the House of Commons, when the government has said that its policy is to prevent a further increase in price levels in this country, with all the warnings that Canada is becoming a high cost economy which is endangering our export trade, I feel the government should consider public ownership of interprovincial pipe lines as a means of securing for Canadian industry energy sources at the lowest possible prices. If energy is brought to Canadian industries at an inflated cost or at an unnecessarily high, cost, then this in turn means that the high cost of energy is passed on in higher and higher prices for finished products. This has a detrimental effect upon the development of the Canadian economy, both from the standpoint of Canadians and also from the standpoint of the development of a healthy export trade.
The government's announced policy is not only a great departure, a complete departure, from the position it has taken in the past, but is in fact very far removed from some of the recommendations made by the royal commission on energy. The report of the commission on energy contains the following recommendation on page 28. This concerns the prices, tolls and rates which should be set by the board of transport commissioners. The recommendation reads as follows:
That the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of a company owning or operating an oil or gas pipe line as regulated by the board of transport commissioners for Canada, should be just and reasonable, nondiscriminatory and calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity, after making due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes.

National Energy Board
The important part of this recommendation, I submit, is that in the opinion of the royal commission tolls, rates and prices than can be charged should be set at levels to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity. Instead of that the government has said they will have the board follow a general policy of setting rates that will provide a fair and reasonable rate of return. These two things are far removed, because the assets of a company very often are so much larger than the shareholders' equity. A company which finances largely by bonds or by debentures is very often able to show a very high rate of return on shareholders' equity; and the announced policy of the government means the continuation, in all probability, of fabulous returns, fabulous profits that have been made from the oil and gas pipe lines of this country.
On page 33 of the energy commission report we find a table showing the percentage return on shareholders' equity in the Trans Mountain pipe-line company. In 1955 the percentage return on shareholders' equity was 27 per cent; in 1956, 43.5 per cent; in 1957, 38 per cent. There were tremendous profits and tremendous returns on the shareholders' equity. The profit of Interprovincial Pipe-line Company, based on a percentage return on shareholders' equity, was in 1953, 18.3 per cent; in 1954, 11.3 per cent; in 1955, 11.5 per cent; in 1956, 18.1 per cent; in 1957, 15 per cent. The percentage return on shareholders' equity in the Montreal Pipe-line Company, and of the Portland Pipe-line Corporation was as follows: 1953, 15.6 per cent; 1954, 9.94 per cent; 1955, 20.45 per cent; 1956, 19.51 per cent; 1957, 14.76 per cent.
These fabulous returns and fabulous profits on pipe lines have made millionaires almost overnight. These profits have accrued not only to Canadians but to United States citizens. These profits have accrued to the Texas buccaneers about whom we heard so much from hon. members opposite when they were in opposition. How they complained about the government's policy with regard to Trans-Canada pipe line company. How they complained that the government was allowing foreign capital to come into this country and make fabulous profits in the development of Canadian natural resources, fabulous profits which were made in a way that was endangering the very sovereignty of this nation, the very control of Canadian industry.
The Prime Minister himself, when he spoke on this subject in the past, has waxed very eloquent. The Prime Minister made many statements on this subject, and on page 4032 of Hansard lor May 17, 1956 he had this to say:

The perquisites here are that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should abdicate his belief in democratic principles and deny those in opposition the right to advance their arguments and to educate public opinion or to find out why there is such solicitude on the part of the members of this government. For five long years this pampered pet, Trans-Canada Pipe-lines, by deviation, by change of direction, by protestation, by alteration in course, has postponed that estimable end of securing a market for Alberta gas and the making available to other parts of Canada of that necessary form of energy. I ask the Prime Minister today to tell this house why he is so fearful of the facts; why he was afraid to allow the true facts of this nefarious scheme to be elucidated? I ask why he found it necessary, and the members of his government found it necessary, to muzzle the representatives of the people in advance of anything in the nature of a filibuster or an interference on the part of the opposition with the policy and program of the government. I ask him to explain that today, for certainly the day of silence is past. Are they afraid of the truth over there? Is that why they hide behind the caricature of parliament which they have substituted by the adoption of the parliamentary form of closure in a way that it has never been adopted before?
A few years ago, Mr. Chairman, the Trans-Canada pipe line scheme was a nefarious scheme in the words of the Prime Minister. The present Minister of Public Works, speaking in the same debate on May 15, 1956, as reported at page 3955 of Hansard said:
I conclude my remarks by this statement, and I make it after careful consideration. I believe that this measure now proposed by the government is the greatest betrayal of the Canadian people since confederation.
This resolution before us assures the continuation of this greatest betrayal of the Canadian people since confederation. The government, instead of going as far as the recommendation of the royal commission on energy to hold down profits to a fair return on shareholders' equity, has left the door wide open for the continuation of these fat and fabulous rates of profit that are accruing from the pipe lines of this country.
This is a complete reversal of the position the government has taken in days gone by. Not only is it a reversal of the position which was taken as far as the Trans-Canada pipe line is concerned; it would appear from the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night to be even much more than that, because the government has shifted its ground from the position it took in parliament in 1956. In those days it was to be Canadian capital developing these resources, but last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say, as reported at page 3767 of Hansard:
We recognize the need for and welcome capital whether domestic or foreign for investment in the energy and associated industries, and we believe such capital, wisely invested, should enjoy a fair and a reasonable rate of return.

That is opening the door wide for United States capital to come in and take over even to a larger extent the operation of pipe lines in this country as well as the control of Canada's energy resources. The government has retreated from the position it took when in opposition. It has now adopted the policy of the former government. It has now put its arms around something it once described as a nefarious scheme. It has now accepted as part of its own policy something that was once described as the greatest betrayal of the Canadian people since confederation, and this announced policy of the government leaves the door open for further betrayals of the Canadian people by a repetition in the future of the scandalous schemes of the past.
Pipe lines in this country, not only the Trans-Canada pipe line and interprovincial pipe lines, seem to be industries in which people make fabulous profits overnight. They seem to be industries in which many actions are taken which should not be condoned and which, apart from the law itself, are very questionable. We know of the pipe line scandals in the province of Ontario. We have read about alleged pipe line scandals in the province of Quebec. We know the way the people in the city of Winnipeg and in the province of Manitoba are being held up by exorbitant prices being charged for the use of natural gas by consumers, all because the Conservative party has turned its back on a policy of public development of these resources.
Public development has been used in the past by various governments as an important means of developing Canadian resources. We have a publicly owned railway. We have the Ontario hydro, which is doing a good job. We have the Manitoba hydro that has pioneered in that province the development and distribution of electrical energy. But the Conservative party has now closed its eyes to the great vision of public development which was once that of the Conservative party.
Out in the province of Manitoba the information I have is that consumers in the city of Winnipeg will have to pay 90 cents per thousand cubic feet of natural gas, a price which is at least 16 cents higher than the price paid by consumers in the province of Saskatchewan even after the additional cost of transportation of the gas is taken into account. In the province of Saskatchewan the distribution of natural gas has been undertaken by the Saskatchewan power corporation, a publicly owned company. Consumers in the city of Regina have to pay 70 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas, but in the city of Winnipeg, although it costs just 4 cents to transport a unit of gas from the city of Regina to the city of Winnipeg, the cost is 90 cents. The province of Manitoba and the
Veterans' Land Act
city of Winnipeg are having to pay rates 20 per cent in excess of the rates paid in Saskatchewan even after one takes into account the cost of transporting the gas for the increased distance, and this 20 per cent is the fee the people of Manitoba have to pay for a policy that is against their own interests and is in favour of private capital, whether Canadian or foreign.
If Canada as a nation, Mr. Chairman, is to develop at a maximum rate, and if our industries are to have access to the cheapest possible power, then the policy the government has announced should now be changed. This is not a policy designed to provide low cost energy in Canada; it is a policy that will result inevitably in more scandal, in the lining of the pockets of more Texas buccaneers, in a further encroachment on Canadian sovereignty by United States capital. This policy announced by the government is the capitulation of the Conservative party to the Texas buccaneers and to the gas and oil barons in this country. This is the disappointing conclusion that the government has arrived at after studying the report of the royal commission on energy and after having been in office for almost two years.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion this policy is uneconomic, it is un-Canadian, and it is a policy that will impose tremendous burdens of additional and unnecessary cost, until checked, on future generations of Canadians. I am surprised and amazed that a government that got to office to a very large extent by exploiting the need to develop Canadian resources by Canadians and by Canadian capital, a party which came to office because it advocated low cost energy sources in this country, should have now made a complete about face and embraced the policy which it once condemned so strongly. By the same token it has condemned Canadians for many years to come to paying exorbitant and excessive rates for energy sources in this country, at the same time turning over larger and larger shares of Canada's energy resources to foreign capital and foreign interests.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

It is my belief that the Veterans' Land Act

Veterans' Land Act
has been the most successful of all the rehabilitation measures that make up the veterans charter. It has been extremely well administered at all levels, and in my opinion the department has been extremely fortunate in recruiting the right type of person to administer this legislation. The officials have always displayed the right attitude. That has been apparent from the beginning and maintained to this day. In all cases the interests of the veterans have been put first, and he has been given good advice even though it was perhaps not in accord with his own wishes.
The success of this phase of veterans legislation is due in large measure, I believe, to the frequent contact there has been between officials and the veterans concerned, and to the follow-up advice and guidance given in solving current problems. The passage of time has brought about changes, however, and many of the provisions in the charter have been rendered out of date. This is particularly true of the financial provisions. Land values have increased and the purchasing power of the dollar has declined, so the financial assistance available under the present legislation is no longer realistic in relation to today's prices.

The extension of the purposes for which grants under this legislation will be used will also be warmly welcomed.
Coming from Newfoundland I am particularly interested in that part of the act that provides for grants to commercial fishermen. I am very pleased to note that the minister is proposing to increase the maximum amount from $1,400 to $3,000.
For some reason or other it appears that the benefits available to commercial fishermen have not proved as attractive as those available to veterans who wish to settle on the land. I do not know what the situation is on the west coast, but it is my impression that in the Atlantic provinces we have not taken as much advantage of this legislation as we might. I hope the publicity that will attend this legislation on its passage through this house will induce more veterans to take advantage of this part of the legislation.
In addition to the changes consequent upon changing conditions there will also be other changes borne out of the experience of the department in administering the act. We hope that as far as the commercial fishermen are concerned the changes contemplated will

bring this legislation in line with the changes that are taking place in the commercial fishing industry.
I am sure that all veterans will appreciate the extension of the benefit period, which will enable those who have not yet been able to take advantage of this legislation and whose time may be running out to have another chance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of Labour) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION NO. 105 CONCERNING THE ABOLITION OF FORCED LABOUR
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve of convention No. 105, concerning the abolition of forced labour which was

adopted by the international labour conference at its fortieth session at Geneva on the 25th day of June, 1957, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to obtain the approval of parliament to a convention adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization in 1957. This is convention No. 105, designated as the convention concerning the abolition of forced labour. I understand that copies of the text of this convention have been distributed to members of the house.
This convention provides that every member state which ratifies it undertakes to suppress and not to make use of any form of forced or compulsory labour as a means of political coercion or education or as a punishment for holding or expressing political views or views ideologically opposed to the established political, social or economic system, as a method of mobilizing and using labour for purposes of economic development, as a means of labour discipline, as a punishment for having participated in strikes, as a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination.
We have no systems of forced labour in Canada, and to the best of our knowledge there is no legislation now in effect in Canada which would be inconsistent with or in contravention of the provisions of the convention. The opinion of the Minister of Justice is that in these circumstances no legislation is required to implement the provisions of the convention. It is hardly necessary for me to say that systems of forced labour are entirely repugnant to our social, economic and political institutions in Canada.
The adoption of this convention on the abolition of forced labour by the international labour conference in June, 1957 was the outcome of inquiries and discussions by and within the United Nations and the international labour organizations over the past ten years. In 1951 an ad hoc committee on forced labour was appointed jointly by the secretary general of the United Nations and the director general of the international labour office as a fact finding body to study the problems raised by the existence in the world of forced labour employed as a means of political coercion or in large scale economic plans. The committee's report in 1953 revealed facts that showed the existence of such systems of forced labour, and established that these systems seriously threatened fundamental human rights and jeopardized the freedom and status of workers.
A proposal to adopt a convention outlawing forced labour was placed on the agenda of the international labour conference for 1956 and 1957. Throughout the discussions

the Canadian delegation, representing government, workers and employers, supported the adoption of a convention which would identify and outlaw the kinds of forced labour which the committee's report had revealed. The convention for the abolition of forced labour was adopted by the 1957 international labour conference with no dissenting votes.
We are asking approval of this convention by parliament in order that we may proceed to ratify the convention immediately thereafter. This convention is an effort by the international labour organization to carry out one of its essential aims of abolishing conditions of labour which involve injustice, hardship and privation to large numbers of people by prevailing upon its member states to eliminate such conditions. A convention which receives a large number of ratifications becomes a powerful force. There is no doubt that Canada should ratify this convention to show our serious interest in and support for the universal abolition of forced labour, which is the objective of the convention.
I feel confident that approval of this convention by parliament will have the support of the vast majority of Canadians. Certainly this is so in the case of Canadian management and organized labour, whose representatives participated and played an active part in the formulation and approval of the convention by the international labour conference. Both these groups have also urged upon the government the ratification of this convention.
For the information of the house I might add that the United Kingdom was the first country to ratify this convention and Denmark was the second. The convention came into force 12 months after two ratifications had been registered, which in this case was January 17, 1959. It has now also been ratified by 18 other countries to date, Austria, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Ghana, Haiti, Honduras, Ireland, Israel, Jordan, Malaya, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, El Salvador, Sweden, Switzerland, Tunisia and the United Arab Republic. I trust that the house will give full support to this resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION NO. 105 CONCERNING THE ABOLITION OF FORCED LABOUR
speechtext:
I have only a word or two to say about this international labour office convention which is number 105 in a long series of conventions which have emanated from that international organization and which have made their contribution to the betterment of labour conditions throughout the world. Indeed, I recall that Canada has ratified a great many of these conventions in the past. On one occasion the government of the day, under Mr. Bennett, thought that these conventions might be used for the passage of social security legislation in this country without reference to the provinces.
This fact persuades me to ask the minister a question in regard to this convention, the purpose of which we are heartily in accord. In asking the minister this question,
I realize that this convention imposes no legislative responsibility, as I understand it, on Canada because as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has just said, none of the obligations in this convention has to be undertaken by us in the sense that the offences covered in the convention do not exist in this country. Nevertheless, the subject matter of this convention is one which, under our construction, falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces. I would ask the


minister, therefore, whether this convention has been considered by or referred to the provinces for their consideration or for any comments they might wish to make concerning it, even though as I understand it no obligation to implement this convention is involved?
I should like also, if I may, to ask the minister-because I have not the information myself-whether, and if so how many, the communist states accepted this convention, and how many middle east Arab states and African states accepted this convention? The minister said when he was introducing the resolution that it had been accepted unanimously at the international labour organization conference called for the purpose of drawing up this convention. This might mean, of course, merely that no country voted against the convention but there might have been a long list of abstentions. Perhaps the minister could give us that information. Article 1 of this convention reads:
Each member of the International Labour Organization-
That includes the Soviet union and other countries now.
-which ratifies this convention undertakes to suppress and not to make use of any form of forced or compulsory labour-
(a)	as a means of political coercion or education or as a punishment for holding or expressing political views or views ideologically opposed to the established political, social or economic system:
(b)	as a method of mobilizing and using labour for purposes of economic development;
(c)	as a means of labour discipline;
(d)	as a punishment for having participated in strikes;
(e)	as a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination.
In view of the social and economic organization of several communist states, and the attitude taken in those states towards free labour, it would be interesting indeed to know whether any communist state has accepted article 1 of this convention or indeed whether it has ratified it. I think the minister said in his opening statement that Poland had ratified the convention.
It would be interesting also to know whether states have accepted and ratified this convention whose labour legislation is so reactionary-and I think of one or two who used to talk about human rights and fundamental freedoms at the United Nations-and whose labour legislation is so reactionary that it is not an exaggeration to say that slavery is recognized in those states. However, that does not detract, Mr. Speaker, from the value of a convention of this kind. The fact that some states could not, without a change in social and economic organization, sincerely accept and carry out a convention of this kind is

no argument that the provisions of this convention should not be embodied in the law elsewhere so far as that is possible. We do, therefore, support the convention as an indication of the direction in which all countries should be moving, namely the abolition of anything that might approach forced labour.
I recall that when this subject used to be discussed, and it was discussed at every United Nations assembly, there was always an attack made by communist members of the United Nations against forced labour in what they called the colonial territories. These were supposed to be the places where forced labour provisions were most used. It was interesting and a little disillusioning to realize that some of the members who used to make the strongest attacks on forced labour in colonial territories under the guise of protecting human rights and fundamental freedoms were those states who had provisions in their own constitutions and who operated their own social and economic organizations in such a way [DOT]that free labour, in our sense of the word, was not possible.
Nevertheless, as I have said, this convention perhaps will help in the movement toward the abolition of forced labour or anything approaching forced labour in any country. At least it is an ideal, and to put the ideal on paper in this way as an International Labour [DOT]Office convention might do some good in those countries where it is most required, some of which I have ventured to mention.

Like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), who naturally has a rather detailed and considerable appreciation of conditions concerning forced labour which exist in other countries in the world, we too abhor very much the attitude and the approach to this retaliatory method of forcing people into certain types of labour because of political or religious beliefs. That has taken place in the Soviet union, and more recently on the mainland of China. Even though this convention does not apply to Canada, we may assist in promoting and setting an example to other countries of the world to follow our lead and allow to the fullest extent possible freedom as we know and understand it. I think that example could not only be
International Labour Conference set for the so-called communist countries but for other countries which are under colonial rule. That situation is changing gradually and I hope will be completely eliminated as the next few years pass by.
As has been indicated, I think the minister could have shown Canada to be much more concerned with the freedom and rights of individuals if he had been able to introduce into the house a motion concerning the en-dorsation or ratification of other I.L.O. conventions, and I have one in particular in mind about which I asked the minister a question some time ago. subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION NO. 105 CONCERNING THE ABOLITION OF FORCED LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that supporting a convention or supporting the abolition of forced labour is almost akin to declaring oneself against sin. It is a sad reflection on the state of our 20th century civilization upon which we pride ourselves so much that such conventions are even necessary.
The purpose of this convention, as with previous conventions, is to spotlight public opinion on this problem of forced labour and to mobilize forces which will tend to eliminate it. This convention which is referred to in the resolution replaces a former one which I think came into existence around 1930. I believe soviet Russia was a signatory to that 1930 convention. One therefore cannot help but wonder what is going to be accomplished by merely declaring ourselves in support of a resolution when countries who are signatories do not even begin to take the matter seriously.
This problem of forced labour is perhaps a bigger one today than it was a generation ago or even two generations ago. We have now forced labour on a massive scale in Red China as a distinct part of government economic policy. We know that forced labour has always existed in Siberia and Russia, and those conditions exist today. If we are going to support a resolution of this kind, surely we should look into it a little further and try to And out exactly what it is we are supporting.
The minister read out different categories of forced labour. There is forced labour for political purposes; forced labour for economic purposes; forced labour for disciplinary or corrective action; and in many countries these are embodied in laws which exist on their own statute books. I think we should ask ourselves where we draw the line in these categories. Does this convention repudiate all forms of forced labour, or does it just repudiate the categories mentioned by the minister? Certainly if we are going to endorse the principle in this debate, as we are by supporting this resolution, we are declaring ourselves against all forms of forced labour which militates against the concept of human rights and the degradation of human beings. Unlike my hon. friends from Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and Skeena (Mr. Howard), I do not see this as a matter of the rights of organized labour; I think it is a matter of human rights.
As far as labour is concerned, I think it is necessary to distinguish between labour that is forced and labour that is not forced. When whole villages are uprooted and mass transportations to other parts of the world are ordered, we know that that is something to


be condemned. We know, also, that when people are herded together in concentration camps, no matter whether for political purposes or corrective action, that is something which we condemn. We cannot say that all labour is bad, because in the case of prisoners of war a certain amount of labour is both necessary and a good thing. What we are concerned with is where to draw the line. I think we are more concerned with the treatment that these men receive. We heard from the Hong Kong veterans in the committee on veterans affairs some while ago, and they told us how they had been subjected to long hours of labour and to physical strains quite beyond human capacity, while living on insufficient food in conditions which provided inadequate shelter, and subject to a complete lack of sanitation and medical care. They told us that the pay which they should have received by international convention for the kind of work they were doing was either given them in worthless money or stolen from them.
We know that these evils against which we declare ourselves cannot be corrected by education alone, though education is certainly a part of the process. If we intend to support the principle of this resolution and then forget about it I do not think we can be regarded as acting in a sincere way. Surely we can do more than that. If we accept this resolution we are imposing upon ourselves an obligation to seize every opportunity to mobilize public opinion against these evils. If we intend to make an effort in this direction we must recognize that these evils are mainly the result of a materialist ideology, an ideology which has been embraced by a large section of the world's population. If we are to do anything about it, we in the west must ourselves develop a superior ideology which will bring about changes in men's hearts from which all these evils flow.

such as Great Britain, Belgium and France. When the hon. gentleman says he has not consulted the provinces, does he not think- and I say this without in any way abridging our desire to ratify this worthy convention- that we should take into account the powers of the provinces as has been done, I am sure, in the past in the case of all these conventions. Of the 18 countries which have ratified this forced labour convention I can only think of one which is a communist country to my knowledge, and that is Poland.

Excise Tax Act

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I must rise at once on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Essex East has indicated he is about to speak on a subject which is completely outside the scope of this bill. There is nothing in this bill which has any bearing on the special excise tax on automobiles. This is simply a bill to amend the Excise Tax Act. We are not on the resolution stage of our discussions, and we are faced with the well-established rule that only those matters which are relevant and which are included in the scope of this amending bill can be the subject of debate.

On the point of order, may I say that the Minister of Finance is again usurping functions which belong, by decision of this house, to you, Mr. Speaker. We are debating the principle of the bill and I am complaining about the fact that this bill does not include relief by way of substantial reduction or elimination of the excise tax on automobiles. There can be no doubt that I am perfectly in order in saying that this bill is deficient in that it does not make provision of a kind which, I am submitting to the house at the present time, it should. I take it that Your Honour agrees with me in recognizing this elementary principle of debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recall that in an earlier parliament a very similar situation arose as a result of an amendment which was accepted as an amendment declaring a contrary principle to the bill.
Last session.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes, last session. It might be possible that the same situation would arise again but generally speaking the matter before the house is the substance of the bill itself and although to my mind it is quite relevant to indicate the deficiencies of the bill I would think it would create very considerable problems for the house if hon. members were to be free to debate at length the various deficiencies which could be ascribed to any tax bill which covers as broad a tax field as the excise tax.
For example, one might raise discussion of 50 or 100 excise taxes which exist and are not covered by this bill. It does not seem to me that the practice of the house would

Excise Tax Act
extend that far. I am not sure how far the hon. member wants to go in this matter but I would think that it would be in order to call attention in a general way to the deficiencies of the bill without getting into an extensive debate on any particular item that is left out unless it could be asserted as it was last year as a contrary principle to the bill. The peculiar circumstances of that case might not pertain today. I do not know if that assists the hon. member or not, but he may proceed.

Your Honour has helped me up to a point but I would be inclined to say that Your Honour has not been as liberal in interpretation as I would think the situation warrants. I would have thought that under this bill any hon. member, no matter how time-consuming, would be allowed to rise and say that this bill was deficient because it does not provide for something which an hon. member felt it should provide. I think that is essential to the right of debate on the principle of the bill at this particular stage of our proceedings. If such intervention can be regularized by way of amendment as it was last year, perforce it could be done by way of a declaration or criticism such as the one I am now about to make to the minister.
Since Your Honour has recognized my right I shall briefly state my position as I tried to do on two other occasions, as the Minister of Finance will recall when we were entering into a discussion of the items that go to make up automobiles and at which time my hon. friend took strong exception to my right to do so. He objected to my discussing this particular matter then, as he does now.
I acceded to his request and am now taking the only course open in this session to put before the minister, other than in the form of interrogation, my complaint which is this. This government promised in my own city and in other communities in Canada that there would be at least a substantial elimination of the excise tax on automobiles. The Prime Minister said that because of the situation then confronting the country in terms of unemployment he would see to it that the tax would be eliminated or at least substantially removed.
He called it a scandalous tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two and one-half per cent.

The minister reduced it by 2J per cent after it was generally thought that the government was about to make a substantial reduction in the tax or eliminate it altogether.
The situation is this. The automobile industry has been confronted with very serious unemployment for some 18 months now. While this problem will not be completely relieved by any further substantial reduction in the excise tax, it would be greatly assisted. This would be an encouragement to many people who are now reluctant to purchase automobiles to do so. The automobile companies have been requesting this as indeed has the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer) who sits behind my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.
We are now discussing in Canada the manufacture of small cars. I note, by the way, that the Minister of Finance has not participated in those discussions. It would seem to me to have been very useful in respect of this particular problem if the Minister of Finance had arranged to be present to have discussions when the heads of these companies met the Prime Minister, one of them today and the three others last Saturday. I ask the Minister of Finance now if he does not think as a means of relieving the serious unemployment problem the elimination of this tax at this time would be very helpful as a contribution in that direction?
If my hon. friend the minister replies he will likely say that when hon. gentlemen opposite came into power the tax was 10 per cent. It is true that the excise tax had been 25 per cent at one time and it was subsequently reduced from 25 per cent to 15 per cent and then to 10 per cent. The head of the previous government in an important statement indicated that if it became evident to the government that the excise tax was a serious obstacle to reducing unemployment his government would not hesitate to take the step which such a situation warranted. That situation now confronts us and indeed it confronted us last year.
As a member of parliament from one of the constituencies heavily involved in this particular problem, a problem that affects thousands of people in an extremely serious way, I would ask the Minister of Finance as one of his last acts in the Department of Finance to accede to this request on the part of one of his dear friends who speaks on behalf of thousands of men who want

me to bring home to the minister at this time their serious plight. The Minister of Finance may shortly have the opportunity of doing something about peace; he now has the opportunity of doing something about giving men employment.

Mr. Speaker, as a native of Norfolk county, I want to reiterate my objection to this bill on the ground that it does the exact opposite of what was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the election campaign, even in the second election which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) still recognizes as having some validity, although he says the promises in the first campaign were all wiped out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All carried out.

Carried out? As the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has pointed out, they were carried out the back door. I should just like to recall to hon. members' minds, in case they have forgotten them since the last time this matter was discussed, some of the promises made by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister made a very specific reference to the tobacco tax at Brantford on February 18, 1958, as reported in a Canadian Press release carried in the Ottawa Journal of that date. The reference is in these words:
He also promised a review of taxes on tobacco, which he described as the heaviest on any industry in Canada.
I also have here a report from a reputable and indeed excellent newspaper, the Windsor Star, which after referring to the price of cigarettes and the tax, quotes the Prime Minister directly as having said:
We are having this whole question looked into. A study is being made to ascertain what action should be taken to give the tobacco farmer a fair and reasonable return.
The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Knowles) speaking in the early election, it is true, but presumably he was still of the same mind in the second election, as reported in the newspaper of his own county the Simcoe Reformer of June 5, 1957, had this to say:
The promises of John Diefenbaker and the Conservative party are not those from an old hat but have been brought up in the parliament time and time again so I say it is time for a change for the benefit of Norfolk and Canada.
That is a direct quotation attributed to the present hon. member for Norfolk. We have had the change for the benefit of Norfolk and the rest of western Ontario and of Canada to which he referred and in addition to the failure to do anything about the motor car tax, to which my friend the hon. member for Essex East referred, we have had this action
Excise Tax Act
on the tobacco tax which was the exact opposite of what was promised and which I think will not be forgotten in western Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised that members of the large government party are not rising at this time to take advantage of the opportunity, on second reading of this bill, to speak as they did on previous occasions when they were sitting on this side of the house. I agree with your ruling that one would not want to go into any particular omission in an exhaustive way with respect to this bill; but, on the other hand, I simply want to remind this house, and particularly new members of the house, that in past debates when another government was in office, at this stage of the debate we heard from the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) and we heard from the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) about the excise tax on automobiles; we heard from the member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) about the excise tax on clocks and watches; we heard from a former member of the Bennett government, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) with respect to the desirability of having no taxes on the purchases by municipalities in the automobile field. We always heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and from the Minister of Finance with respect to the elimination of taxes on what they called the necessities of life and they referred to boots and shoes, clothing and the like. None of these things was either in the legislation that was proposed in 1957 and 1958, or that which is proposed now. We heard from many members who showed no indication of rising at this time with respect to some other matters that are not referred to in the bill we have before us. I think of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) who referred to municipal purchases. I think of the Minister of Finance who has forgotten some of his views in the past with respect to municipal purchases.
We, of course, always expected on this particular bill to have a very informative and helpful speech from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) with respect to the automobile industry. That has not been forthcoming. I think, too, of the lack of any interest on the part of those in the majority party today because seemingly they do not want to rise to say anything in this debate. I think of what they said in the past with respect to the elimination of sales tax obligations for welfare associations. Nothing has been said today by any of those people in that respect. I think particularly of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) who used to make

Excise Tax Act
speeches when he was in opposition about this. I wonder whether he has been making representations to the Minister of Finance and, if so, why they have not been successful?
I think, too, about the over-all rate. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) in past years repeatedly used to assert that the actual percentage rate was unconscionable and should be reduced. I could refer to some speeches of this nature that he made in the past. But, Mr. Speaker, we are not hearing them today and indeed there was no attempt on anybody's part from the government party to rise to say anything on any of these matters that formerly seemed to be of concern to them.
I am not going to amplify what was said about the tobacco tax by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), but we know that there was no bailiwick in Canada from coast to coast where there was an economic problem too insignificant for the Prime Minister to make pronouncements about in the elections of 1957 and 1958 and, as has been referred to, he was particularly vocal when near Norfolk county and speaking in Brantford on this particular subject.
This is the third stage of discussion of changes in our tax system as announced in the budget. Therefore, I do not want to over-emphasize some of those points. I have spoken upon some of them in the past, but I do want to say as briefly as I possibly can that the legislation we are now dealing with, which is one bill out of five resulting from the budget proposals, does in the words of taxpayers represent chickens coming home to roost kind of legislation. It spells out very well the kind of thing that I want to convey to this house. Somebody else has said that with respect to two election campaigns, after the ball is over, why, of course, now we are seeing in tax proposals many hearts broken. That, I think, is very much exemplified in this one of five bills that have been presented to us, all of which involve additional imposts on the Canadian taxpayers. We are dealing now with sales tax on municipal purchases, or the absence of any benefit for them. One of the ironical things that I think most of us noted was that even though all of the Canadian municipalities through their nationl organization called upon this government, we found that no relief was granted when the budget was announced, notwithstanding the many suggestions that had been made in the past by members of the present administration, as I have illustrated.
It is true that in this particular bill the consumer tax is not impressively raised. It was most impressively raised as a result of using the Excise Tax Act statute as a basis

for the over-all 1 per cent increase and the amendment to the Old Age Security Act. I am not going to refer to that except to say that that was a very large increase in taxation upon the Canadian people. The Minister of Finance and I had something in the nature of a difference during the budget debate on this particular point and I said that taxes- and I had reference to corporation taxes- that were likely to be passed on to consumers were a very substantial portion of the overall $352 million annual increase proposed in this budget. Mr. Chairman, before this clause carries, I think it might be well if I were to make a few remarks concerning this bill. The Canadian Legion was first organized under the Companies Act by a charter granted by the secretary of state on July 17, 1926. It is rather interesting to note that the present amendments have been submitted to the parliamentary counsel, Dr. Maurice Ollivier, Q.C., who in 1926 drafted the original charter. It was the successor to the great war veterans' association and other original ex-servicemen's bodies which were formed after world war I. The latter half of the title includes the name of the parent organization to which the Canadian Legion belongs, even though it is practically an autonomous body in Canada.
There was no change in the original charter until May 14, 1948, when the Legion was incorporated by a private act of parliament, being chapter 84 of the statutes of Canada. The official title of the Legion remained unchanged, but the various provisions necessary for the proper functioning of the organization as a large nation-wide body, which it had become after the heavy influx of veterans from world war II, were spelled out. This legislation brought it in line with bodies of similar size scope functioning on a dominion-wide basis.

In 1951 a few amendments were made to the act of incorporation, pertaining mostly to minor changes in the by-laws and restrictions on the use of legion insignia. Bill No. S-19 recommends several changes which are required at the present time but which do not change the original purpose or setup of the present organization.
Clause 1 merely changes the legal name of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League to the Canadian Legion. It will be noted from the bill that this change of name does not "in any way impair, alter or affect the rights or liabilities of the legion." The principal reason for this request was the recent change in the name of the parent organization to the British Commonwealth Ex-Services League, and the possibility of another change at a future date. This would naturally be an upsetting factor and create again considerable confusion and expense, so it was decided to adopt the simple title of "The Canadian Legion".
Clause 2 makes identical and necessary alterations to accommodate the ladies auxiliary of the Legion by striking out the words "of the British Empire Service League" in paragraph (r) of section 4 of chapter 84 of the statutes of 1948.
The intention of clause 3 is to enlarge the objects of the Legion. A perusal of the present purposes and objects as given in the explanatory notes of the bill indicates that they are particularly related to the problems and welfare of the veteran and his dependents, perpetuation of the fallen, fostering loyalty and education in the principles of patriotism, duty and unstinted public service, as well as many other matters pertaining to veterans' affairs exclusively. In this field members of the Legion have done a magnificent job. Motivated by the same high purposes and spirit of unselfish sacrifice which prompted them to serve their country in time of emergency, they have carried on a great work of voluntary service on behalf of their fellow veterans all across the nation.
If I were to pay the proper tribute to the Legion, a great deal of time would be required, and I am sure that is not necessary. Members of this house, many of whom are veterans and active members of the Legion, as well as most of our Canadian people, daily witness the great work being carried out by its members. This organization enjoys the standing of being one of the largest and most respected groups in the country, and now numbers almost a quarter of a million members. It has been somewhat confined, however, in its activities and in the use of its name beyond the purposes outlined by the present act.

In order to participate officially and more widely in other affairs, it is requested that its objects be enlarged by adding to section 4 of chapter 84 of the statutes of 1948, the following paragraph (v):
(v) "To encourage, promote, engage in or support all forms of national, provincial, municipal or community service, or any charitable or philanthropic purpose."
Clause 4 would amend section 6 of chapter 84 of the statutes of 1948, as amended by chapter 86 of the statutes of 1951 (first session), and would provide for more flexibility in the internal operation and efficiency of the Legion. Conventions are held only every second year, and it can be readily realized that considerable business must be carried on by the executive council, which is the governing body between conventions. This clause provides for an extension of powers to the executive council from the dominion convention more in line with the 1948 statutes. It should be noted that there is ample safeguard for any action taken by the executive council, as such action must be placed before a subsequent convention and ratified or modified to remain effective, or it can be deleted if the convention so wishes.
Private Bills
necessary for the Canadian Legion to make corresponding changes in the name of the Canadian organization.
The membership of the Canadian Legion, of course, is formed from members of Her Majesty's services and auxiliary services who have served in a theatre of war and who have been honourably discharged. The primary objective of the Canadian Legion has always been to look after the welfare of veterans, their families and dependants. To this end they have raised funds and assisted veterans with advice, and in various ways according to the need. They have also assisted various governments with advice in connection with veterans' legislation. In this connection too they have always made a special point of looking after the burial of deceased veterans and seeing that they are buried with due ceremony and given a funeral service in which their wartime service is commemorated. The Legion has sponsored an annual poppy fund every year and the proceeds of this fund are devoted to the vetcraft industries which have afforded employment to a great many veterans who otherwise would not be able to make a living.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, probably I should point out to the committee that these changes have been requested by the Legion and were passed at its last dominion convention as recommended by the committee on constitution and laws of the Legion.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon.
member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) has just pointed out, this is a very simple bill which merely proposes to change the name of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League and its related auxiliaries and to enlarge the scope of the activities of their organization.
The Canadian Legion, as everyone knows, is a patriotic, non-sectarian, non-political organization of Canadian service men and service women. Following world war I Canadian veterans banded themselves together into an organization which was known as the great war veterans' association. In 1925, following a visit from Earl Haig to Canada, it at once decided to change its name to the Canadian Legion, and as the hon. member has pointed out, this organization became incorporated under a dominion charter in 1926. The new organization then affiliated itself with the British legion and other similar organizations in various parts of the commonwealth which became known as the British Empire Service League. The British Empire Service League has recently changed its name, and that in turn has made it
66968-9-241J
One of the most important activities of the Canadian Legion during the last war and in the postwar period was the institution of the Canadian Legion educational service. This was a brave experiment in adult education in the armed forces which was eminently successful and which set the pattern which was followed by many countries after the war. The inauguration of this service enabled many veterans to improve their educational standing and even to acquire knowledge of a technical nature during their spare time in the armed services. I think that has paid great dividends to Canada in the development of our human resources, which after all are the most precious resources that any country possesses.
In addition to the welfare of the veterans, the second great objective of the Canadian Legion has been to keep alive the spirit of comradeship and to keep before the nation those traditions and ideals for which our comrades fought and died. We are now approaching a period where the business of looking after the welfare of veterans will perhaps diminish, because already in this session we have revised certain legislation providing benefits to veterans, and only today we passed a resolution concerning the Veterans' Land Act. So it is clear that in the future veterans' welfare will be very well taken care of, and the Legion's efforts in this respect will be confined mainly to those veterans who need assistance and who for some

Private Bills
reason or other are not eligible to receive assistance under the various acts of the veterans' charter.
As the role of welfare diminishes, the role of leadership in the nation will increase. We are living today in a world of ideological conflicts, and we see every day that our values are disappearing before our very eyes, the very values for which so many of our comrades fought and died. We all know that the first world war was fought to end all wars. The big slogan in those days was, "Might is Right". Our comrades fought and died because they believed that might was not right, but that slogan is widely accepted today in many parts of the world, and even in the United Nations we find big countries doing things just because of the sheer weight of their military might and we have to accept and tolerate it because we feel we cannot do much else about it.
One of the big contributions which I feel the Legion can give to this generation of Canadians and to succeeding generations is to revive the emphasis on the moral principles which inspired so many of our comrades and for which so many of them paid the supreme sacrifice. As the hon. member for Kings has pointed out, clause (c) of this bill will enlarge the scope of their community and national activities, and we welcome that. But I think that their main role in the future must be the role of moral leadership, and just as the Legion has been a tremendous force for good in the past so it can become an even greater force for good in the future.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN LEGION OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE SERVICE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the explanation of the purpose of this bill given by the hon. member for Kings and his outline of the activities of the Legion and its history. I well remember joining the old great war veterans' association in 1919, and I am a charter member of the Canadian Legion. Naturally I have taken an active part in that organization since its formation and I am fully aware of the excellent work being done and which has been done for veterans and their dependants throughout the years. Since coming to this house I have been more particularly concerned with their representations before the veterans affairs committee.
I should also say that the Legion does keep alive the spirit of comradeship. When you have stood alongside a chap in the face of heavy fire in the field, it promotes a bond between you which is very difficult to dissolve; in fact, it rarely is dissolved, fortunately. The purpose of clause 1 is to change the name, to meet, I assume, changing constitutional circumstances within the commonwealth. I am going to be quite frank
IMr. Carter.]
and say I am very sorry to see that the name is to be Canadian Legion only. I cannot understand why it is not to be the Canadian Legion of the British Commonwealth Ex-servicemen's League, because I think the ex-servicemen's organization is one of the best cementing influences between the various countries of the commonwealth.
I am a firm believer in the value of the commonwealth in the world today, and in the major and continuing role it can play in world affairs.
I presume there is some valid reason for the omission at this time, but as a member of the Canadian Legion I say that I look forward in the near future to the introduction of another amending bill which will complete the name of the Canadian Legion by calling it the Canadian Legion of the British Commonwealth Ex-servicemen's League.
The second major change in this bill, as I see it, is to enlarge the objects of the Legion as outlined in section 3 which reads:
To encourage, promote, engage in or support all forms of national, provincial, municipal or community service, or any charitable or philanthropic purpose.
I think that this is, in fact, merely giving legal status to activities which have been going on in the Legion throughout the years. And why have these activities been in effect? The answer is this: because the membership of the Canadian Legion and its auxiliaries are people who have a sense of responsibility to Canada and to their communities, and on that account for many years past their activities have extended far beyond the primary objectives of the Legion, which are the welfare of veterans and the welfare of their dependants.
I know that our provincial command is engaged in a number of province-wide activities at the present time. One of them is devoted particularly to the welfare and guidance of youth. As far as our branches in Kootenay West are concerned-they are very active branches-donations-and they are not small donations in relation to the size of the branch in question-are made periodically to hospitals. Legion branches have also undertaken activities for the welfare of our aged citizens. They have assisted voluntary fire brigades in small and incorporated communities by undertaking financial drives; they have helped to develop local libraries; they have taken part in local celebrations; and they have interested themselves in the development of recreation grounds and the raising of money for the development of small parks which are of value to the district in which they are situated. They have also assisted in the building of curling rinks.

Quite recently the zone council of the Canadian Legion in Kootenay West has become very interested in promoting sports for young people on a district-wide basis as a valuable contribution to the welfare and development of our young citizens, and to this end in the very near future we are going to have the first Legion-sponsored sports in the West Kootenay district. The ladies' auxiliaries have also been singularly active. In most cases they have co-operated with the local Legion branches in efforts such as I have just described. All through the years, this kind of activity has gone on. There seems to be a greater activity in the smaller communities than in the larger towns, because there is not the same number of smaller organizations and less tendency for a person's activities and energies to be divided into so many diverse channels.
I say once again that in my opinion this part of the bill simply gives legal status to a situation which has existed in the Canadian Legion and its branches for many years. In conclusion, I wish to repeat that I trust the hon. member will soon introduce a further amending bill which will complete the name of the Canadian Legion as the Canadian Legion of the British Commonwealth Exservicemen's League, as one of the major organizations in the commonwealth today.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-15 to amend the Indian Act.
He said: I have but few comments to make in speaking to the second reading of this particular bill. As the title indicates its purpose is to amend the Indian Act. Inasmuch as we have established a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate which will be holding its first meeting tomorrow morning it would seem appropriate that either the bill itself or the subject matter should be referred to that committee for consideration. However, if this course does not meet the wishes of the house I am sure that some of the members present would like to take this opportunity of expressing their views with regard to the particular amendments which are now proposed, and this in itself may be of some guidance to the joint committee on Indian affairs when it begins consideration of these particular sections of the Indian Act.
While the amendment itself relates to the question of income tax exemptions for Indians in certain circumstances its main purpose is to implement a proposal which I have made in three successive sessions regarding the right of native Indians to vote in federal elections.
Subsection (2) of section 86 of the Indian Act allows for one arrangement by which Indians may have the opportunity of voting in federal elections. It is my purpose to repeal this subsection so that an Indian desiring the right to vote would not have to sign away his statutory right to income tax exemption in respect of the use of reserve land. Perhaps I should read the pertinent portions of section 86. Section 86, subsection 1, reads in part:
Notwithstanding any other act of the parliament of Canada or any act of the legislature of a province,

but subject to subsection (2) and to section 82, the following property is exempt from taxation, namely,
(a)	the interest of an Indian or a band in reserve or surrendered lands, and
(b)	the personal property of an Indian or band situated on a reserve,-
The section then goes on to make reference to succession duty, inheritance tax, and so on.
An extensive study was given to the Indian Act by a committee of this house in 1951. When some hon. members of the present government were in opposition they clearly expressed their opinion as being that the subsection to which I have referred should be deleted from the act. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was a member of the committee in 1951 as was the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton). The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) also made comments about this section and expressed their desire to have it repealed or deleted. I am sure they are of the same opinion today and that they were not making a purely political speech expressing an attitude that may change depending on which side of the chamber one finds oneself occupying. I am convinced that the attitude they expressed in 1951 was sincere.
I submit that subsection (2) of section 86 applies to very few native Indian people. The great majority of Indians earn their livelihood from fishing, logging or other occupations not confined to the reserve. If an Indian earns his income from commercial fishing for instance, he is in the same position as any other fisherman and must pay tax on the income he receives. The same is true of logging or any other occupation. The exemption applies only to the use of reserve land or income received for its use. In order to have the right to vote an Indian must waive his right to that exemption.
The most significant point about this question is the psychological attitude of the Indian. An Indian does not like to sign away, give up, or have taken away any right he may have. It is not important to an Indian whether or not those rights are applicable in an individual case. An Indian looks upon the signing of the waiver form as an example of the white man asking him to give away some of his hereditary, aboriginal or treaty rights. We know that it is a statutory question having no relationship to treaty rights. This is a justifiable attitude based on the experience of Indians with white people over the years. It is immaterial to the Indian whether or not he will earn any money on the reserve and in all probability only a few would be affected by these provisions. The Indian considers it an attempt on the part of white men to take from him a part of his hereditary, aboriginal or treaty rights.
Indian Act
Indians are suspicious of the attitude of non-Indians with respect to their rights and this, I submit, is justifiable because we have a record of shameful exploitation of Indians, their resources and their rights. If we were to remove this section from the act the Indians would consider it an act of good faith on our part as non-Indians indicating that we do not want to interfere with their hereditary, aboriginal or treaty rights. It would indicate that we would want to go half way toward meeting him, and seek to achieve an understanding of his background, history and culture as we insist he understand and accept ours. This action in my opinion would be an act of good faith such as should have been demonstrated by our forefathers in their dealings with the native Indian people. These are the only remarks I have to make at this stage.
