Mr. Speaker, as I understood the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) this bill represents one step toward giving the franchise to the original inhabitants of Canada in that it will protect them from surrendering certain rights when they wish to vote in federal elections. In examining the speech made by the hon. member last year as reported at page 1009 of Hansard of June 10, 1958, I have reached the conclusion that the premise on which the hon. member seeks to obtain the vote for Indians is wrong. On that occasion the hon. member stated:
In my view this matter is important to the welfare of our Indian people. It would be a first step toward assisting them and our people to appreciate and understand each other's ideas and cultures to a greater degree than we have in the past.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS BIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: Can the hon. member tell us what was under consideration at that time?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS BIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
At that time the house was discussing Bill No. C-8 to amend the Canada Elections Act which was moved by the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member made a statement about the psychological attitude of the Indians. In my constituency I have two rather large reservations, and I have practised amongst them for many years and on other reservations as well. Having seen many Indians I can understand the psychological attitude. The Indian still has a very defensive attitude toward the white man. Any time that you give the Indians anything they begin to look for the joker or the nigger in the woodpile. In this instance I would like to know more fully than the hon. member has been able to explain to us what the general attitude of the Indian is toward this modification or amendment to give him the franchise in the future.

Indian Act
As he well knows, in Manitoba we enfranchised the Indians in 1954. Any observations that I have to make along this line will be personal, of course. I find that the Indian has not taken great advantage of that enfranchisement other than the fact that he may now enter the white man's pub. I feel that that is no advancement in so far as culture is concerned, at least. I find that he is not too impressed with the political field provincially.
In the past few months we have had practically a revolution in the Six Nations down near Brantford who would, I am sure, rather abdicate or secede from the dominion than accept any further kindnesses from the great white chief. I should like to say this. Since a committee is being set up, I would rather see this question gone into more fully, to have witnesses brought from all parts of Canada particularly, as the hon. member for Skeena has said, in view of this psychological attitude of the Indian.
No doubt in his own case he has known many Indians and has had some dealings with them. In my own case I do know it is very difficult to approach the Indian and to get his real feelings on anything about which you may want to deal with him or to treat him in a different way. He has this defensive attitude and I am sure that after deliberation in committee we shall have to be sure that they will understand exactly what we are giving them before we ever try to give them the vote federally. Too often, as he has said, in the past what we have given with our left hand we have taken away with our right. Therefore, rather than see this bill debated and voted on today, I would like to see it given a great deal more examination and a great deal more thought.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS BIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am heartily in agreement actually with the comments made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for I, too, feel that the privilege of voting in federal elections particularly should be extended to the Indians who are, after all, our first Canadians. For too long the Indian population of Canada has been sheltered and protected as wards of the crown, until their desire to make decisions of their own has almost gone. However, with better educational facilities being provided for their children by the government and religious organizations and the resultant higher level of education being attained by each succeeding generation, our Indian populations in Canada have begun to wish to do their own thinking and to make their own decisions in more and more matters pertaining to themselves and to their affairs.

I would like also to put on record here the expression of my sincere appreciation for the work of the priests and the sisters of the Oblate Order in the education of the Indian children and people in my constituency more particularly. As is well known to hon. members, various provinces have in varying degrees in the past few years been extending to the Indians the privilege of full citizenship and in some of these provinces these Indians are allowed to vote in provincial elections. That is not so, however, in Alberta.
Most of the Indian problems are of a social nature. In the past they have been particularly educational problems. We as a government in Canada have a responsibility to the Indians in this matter. If I may, I should like to say to the hon. member for Skeena, as I did when I began my remarks, that I am in particular agreement with this problem. To me it is probably a little more serious than it is to him.	I think
there are many things that come before the problem of the franchise, particularly that of education. Indians have not only the problem of assimilating Canadian education but also the terrific problem, as the hon. member who spoke before me mentioned, of retaining their own particular Indian culture. This culture is not only valuable to themselves but it is a valuable addition to Canadian culture, and it is certainly one to be retained if for no other reason than a purely historical one.
In talking to members of the Blood band of Indians from Cardston, which is in my constituency-naturally it is the only one with which I am particularly familiar-I found that they almost unanimously endorse the thought of the franchise for Canadian Indians. But before you much more than commence to talk about the subject you are suddenly brought face to face with the many other problems that the Indians have, everything indeed from the liquor laws to the desperate attempt to retain their own culture.
I would like to submit to hon. members that in my humble opinion, and from my experience with the Blood band of Indians in Alberta, we must consider those other problems. In other words, first problems must come first. I can well imagine Indians being given the franchise. In fact, you might compare it to a young bird or a young child being turned loose in the world without being properly prepared to fend for itself. There are a few Indian people who I understand have attained Canadian citizenship on their own initiative. They have been enabled to do this by a sort of sponsorship. When I mention the word I mean simply this. It is very hard for an Indian person to go out into the everyday life of Canada and educate

himself to the point where he can convince the proper authorities that he is ready for full Canadian citizenship.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to dwell for a moment on the Blood Indians and their particular problems with respect to education. Certainly if we as members of the House of Commons are to enable them to continue or improve their education we must as well take a look at our own methods and standards. The Blood Indian reserve has a population of some 2,500 of our first citizens of the highest order and also, I might add, with problems of the first magnitude. The Indians on the Blood reserve are a very fine and proud people, particularly proud of one of their own who was appointed not long ago to the Senate. This appointment did a great deal for the Indians of Canada. It gave them a renewed interest in the government of Canada and a new zeal to become more useful, better informed and respected members of the Canadian family.
The Indians of the Blood reserve have many problems, as I mentioned before, and I should like to take a moment to point out some of the troubles of this band. I feel this is very closely integrated with the problem of citizenship. Incidentally, I do not mean to criticize our Canadian Indians in any way in this house. Rather, the criticism is of the Canadian government and when I say "Canadian government" I assure hon. members that I am speaking generally.
With these Indians, as with most of us, the chief social interest, of course, is the education of their young people and the need of increased facilities for improvement and refinement in the manner in which this is carried out. May I point out something that is now and has been for some time of great concern to our friends on the reservations in Canada, namely that educational standards are almost completely and entirely those of the white man, neglecting to consider the fact that these people on the reservations have a certain culture and way of life which it is very important to them to retain, and for us to enable them to do so would be most welcome.
Perhaps I might take a moment to refer to Canadian education, and I think this is relevant to the matter under debate. It would be desirable for Canada that a uniform standard of education prevail regardless of whether different regions are economically favoured, and certainly our reservations must be considered in this light. I would hope that educational opportunity for Canada's future citizens will soon be on an equal basis in all parts of the country. I would hope that before long the federal government would find a way to provide support and 66968-9-242
Indian Act
leadership throughout Canada for the purpose of establishing a basic standard of education in all provinces through some financial support and by providing leadership that will equalize every province's ability to provide this basic standard. Certainly this must carry down to the reservations to fill the great need of our Canadian Indians today.
The need for such assistance has been proven beyond doubt to all those in Canada at present interested in education by the very great percentage of high school students entering universities who are having so much trouble with reading, writing and arithmetic. There should be a way for the federal government to provide leadership to all Canadians to solve this national problem which is rapidly becoming one of great concern to the people of the nation for, as some have said, our very survival is at stake and the days of grace are few. Some have also said, and I can see no reason to question their judgment, that our very way of life cannot be expected to survive longer than a period of from 25 to 50 years unless important steps are soon taken to remedy this situation.

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will move into another class of

It is a class which could not, by the wildest stretch of the imagination, be considered as a luxury. I am now referring specifically to toothpaste. First is the matter of the excise tax on motor cars. I am not going into that because we had a debate on that matter a year ago, and we had another debate on it in the session previous to that. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is wrong in ascribing to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) the statement that that tax would be removed. Reference was made to the application of the sales tax to certain purchases by municipalities. I would remind the house that at the 1958 session in the budget proposals we removed the tax on a wide range of purchases by municipalities.
The fourth and last matter to which I shall make brief reference is the subject introduced by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) when he asked about the over-all revision of the Excise Tax Act and alluded to the report of the Carter committee. I think this was a proper matter to be introduced in the debate on second reading, because it is a matter of a general nature applicable to any amending bill which has any relationship at all to those matters which were embraced within the scope of the reference to the Carter committee. I would say that in general many of the provisions of the present bill are in line with the recommendations of the so-called Carter committee which submitted its report to my predecessor, Mr. Harris, on January 12, 1956. Indeed, in the budget speech at page 2422 of Hansard I made reference specifically to one of the important provisions in this bill which stems directly from the report of the Carter committee in reference No. 3 in its report; that is the reference having to do with the tax

Excise Tax Act
on packaging. One could point to a number of other provisions in this bill which are in line with or have been inspired by the report of the Carter committee.
Mr. Speaker, would the minister permit a question. When he says specific changes in this bill, would he relate them to the sections, or perhaps later in the debate do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member
spoke on this subject on April 22 when the resolution was under discussion, and his remarks will be found at page 2950 of Hansard. There he expressed the view that this provision created discrimination between retailers. I hope I can set his mind at rest on that point.
First, I should like to point out that care has been taken in this provision to make certain that retailers who package in their own retail stores and sell directly to consumers through such stores are not affected by these proposed changes. In other words, retailers do not become manufacturers if the packaging is done by them in such conditions. However, any retailer who packages with a view to selling other than directly to consumers becomes a manufacturer. This means that anyone, including a retailer, who does packaging at a central point, say in his warehouse, with a view to selling or transferring the packaged goods to his own retail stores or to other retail stores becomes the manufacturer of such goods. Therefore, when retailers buy either from packagers or directly from a person who fully manufactured cosmetics or pharmaceuticals, the tax will be applied at the same level in the distribution process.
These resolutions are in fact aimed at a discrimination which has been occurring at a different level than that of retailers-one that occurs between the manufacturer who carries out the complete process of manufacturing, including packaging, and one who divides the manufacturing process between himself and others. The latter in this way has been paying the tax and at a much lower level than the person who fully manufactures. This tax inequality was pointed out by the Carter sales tax committee, and these resolutions are based on the recommendations of that committee for the removal of this discrimination. The purpose is to provide a more uniform base for the tax.
Since the cost of packaging and advertising these products represents such a large proportion of the final selling price, a tax levied on these products manufactured for sale in bulk or imported in bulk is considerably less than a tax levied on the sale price of a Canadian manufacturer of similar products who also packages and advertises these products. This means that the Canadian
Excise Tax Act
manufacturer is put at a disadvantage in competing with products imported in bulk for packaging and distribution in Canada. He is also at a disadvantage in competing with a distributor in Canada who has products made up in bulk for him to package and distribute under his own brand name or trademark.
Accordingly the definition of manufacturer is now extended to include any person who packages toilet preparations, cosmetics or pharmaceuticals for sale, except where this is done in a retail store for sale directly to consumers. The definition of manufacturer will also be amended to include any person who markets toilet preparations, cosmetics or pharmaceuticals made up for him to be sold under his own private brand, except a retailer who sells directly and exclusively to consumers or users.
I might point out that this principle of regarding packagers as manufacturers has been in the law for years in applying the special excise tax on cosmetics, and the same principle has also been in the law with respect to sales tax on candy.
I recall the remarks made by the hon. member on April 22. I think, if I may say so, that he did not appreciate then that once a packager becomes a manufacturer under the proposed amendments, he becomes a licensed manufacturer. This means that he may buy his supplies, either bulk or partly manufactured goods, under his licence, without any payment of tax at that time. The tax will then apply on his sales of the packaged or finished article in the same way as it applies to the sale of goods of a manufacturer who carries out all the manufacturing processes himself.

I wish to thank the minister for that explanation. My conclusion is that a sales tax is not paid to the manufacturer but that it is paid to the government at packaging level. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-48, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, we are now discussing a bill very similar to the previous bill, one of five related to the budget. I was amazed that on the introduction of this bill there was not the same enthusiasm and applause on the part of the overwhelming majority that we have heard in this house for the minister's suggestion. I think this results from the fact that after reflection they realized that the budget speech involved the kind of thing upon which we are now asked to legislate. We have 10,000 more civil servants to pay for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is not true.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can support that. There is great inconsistency on the part of the minister in his desire to keep down costs. I pointed out on budget night that all these elements of taxation would enter into the cost of products and would perhaps reduce our opportunity to sell in competitive markets abroad. I think that the bill we have before us is very consistent with that fact.
I also said in the past and I repeat that we are not only concerned with the fact that this particular bill and the other four we have dealt with involve an over-all tax load on the Canadian people for the current year of $245 million but we are concerned with the fact that the minister's own statements indicate that the take from the Canadian people in the current fiscal year is $640 million more than in the past year and the highest of any year of which we have any recollection. I am not projecting these figures for a full year with respect to the taxes involved in this amending bill.
I also want to remind the minister and all my colleagues in the house that when I say that in the current year Canadian taxpayers in aggregate are being asked to find another $640 million for the government this has no relation whatsoever to the legislation we dealt with last week respecting unemployment insurance which involved another $75 million for the taxpayers of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether my friend has concluded this part of his remarks or whether he proposes to go on developing this theme, but obviously this is a budget speech he is making.

He is talking about the over-all balance of ways and means and questions of that kind and here we are dealing with a bill to amend the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would indicate for the guidance of the Chair what is the principle of the bill. It is a bill to increase certain income taxes and to make various detailed amendments to the act, as I understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly so, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am one who, as I have said before, does not want to take undue time to repeat what has been said at an earlier stage, but we are being asked to consider a bill which increases the taxes on persons and corporations and I say that the reason for it is that the government has had no idea of economy. I think that is a very legitimate criticism. In other words, we are getting in this bill the harvest of the election promises that were seeded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and his colleagues in recent times.
Having in mind Your Honour's ruling, and I approve of it, we cannot complain too much except by way of illustration about things which are not in the amending bill that has been presented to us. But there are so many things that are not here that I think we have every reason to examine the bill closely. I think the house will recognize that this is just one of five bills and therefore we cannot be limited too much with regard to the overall extra tax take that is contemplated.
I suggest to the house that we are on very dangerous ground even if we accept what the minister says that, granted no inflation, granted no war, granted several other things, the gross national product may increase in the next year by $2,200 million. The minister is proposing, as a result of this bill and the other four we have been discussing, to take out of that increased productivity $640 million plus $75 million for the unemployment insurance fund, and I pose the question to all hon. members who have to vote upon this legislation whether or not that is an undue proportion of the possible increase in the gross national product for the forthcoming year.
When we come to the clauses of the bill I am going to deal with some other features of the legislation now before us. I think one of the most unnecessary and silliest features of the bill is the amendment advocated by the minister that we should no longer include in medical expenses the amount that is paid by the duly authorized agent of the taxpayer. This is another prime example of the somersault on the part of the minister. He always
Income Tax Act
advocated the elimination of the 3 per cent floor. I have said before and I repeat that surely the basic cost to start with in the case of any taxpayer is the hospital account. The right to claim that for purposes of exemption is being removed and therefore I say that any other adjustments to the Income Tax Act are straight camouflage and are not treating the taxpayer in a fair and square manner. The minister is removing the base upon which the taxpayer has been able to make a claim for exemption and I suggest to the minister that when he takes away the opportunity to claim for purposes of exemption the hospital bill paid in the past by a duly authorized agent, government or insurance company or otherwise, the other amendments he is proposing are completely meaningless and, to extend my term, I think they are a fraud.

Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say a few words at this time on this particular bill. It appears to me that this bill follows very closely in line with most of the legislation that has been introduced by this government. It is a modern Tory variety of the old army stew consisting of equal parts of horse and rabbit-one horse and one rabbit. We have in this legislation rabbit that is good and horse that is bad. Sometimes we have a bigger horse and sometimes we have a smaller rabbit but it is always in equal proportions.
One thing that I think is driven home to the people is this. No matter how much you try to dress it up, there is one cold hard fact which stands out, namely that taxes are up along with interest rates and along with many other things that are rising day by day. It is true, of course, that wages are rising in certain cases, but it is also equally true that in many other cases they are not rising. One thing that seems to be ignored as completely by this government as it was by the last one is that in conjunction with these rising costs and rising taxes there should be a rise in the exemptions. If the cost of living is higher, surely the basic tax exemption should also be higher in order to correspond with the cost of living. This factor, of course, has been ignored again and I think it is most unfortunate that such is the case.
Another thing that disturbs me, Mr, Speaker, is the change that we have with regard to the exemption for medical expenses. I think everybody in this country was agreed that some changes were due. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) mentioned one. I certainly think that the people of this country were not looking for the changes that were made. I am a bit concerned as to just what effect this

Income Tax Act
change is going to have. To a great many people it appears to be a bit discriminatory against the very hospitalization plan that has been advocated and, in fact, finally implemented by this present government, although it was put in the process of implementation by the previous government.
I understand the deductions will remain the same as they were in the past, with medical insurance through private companies but that as to the hospital insurance through the federal and the provincial hospital insurance plan the basic exemption will no longer be under the same formula. I sometimes wonder whether it might not be much easier for the wage earners of this country if they could just deduct the premiums paid to the hospital insurance plan or to a private insurance company from their actual costs of hospital and medical insurance. I am sure it would simplify the tax form considerably. It might save many people a great deal of money by not having to go and get a lawyer or a chartered accountant or someone else to make out their income tax forms. There would be a saving in two or three ways. But in the main I should like to sum up my few remarks by saying that regardless of how well it may be dressed up this bill is just a little bit more bad news to the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, the increase in the personal income tax is quite considerable. It amounts to two percentage points on everything over $3,000. I was a little bit surprised at this increase because the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is reported to have said that every family in Canada was overtaxed by $120. I think I saw some references to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) also having said that taxes were too high and should be reduced. I can say that in my part of the country he has in effect been right because a good many of these people have been unemployed practically ever since and have not had to pay any income taxes at all. When a person fills out his income tax form and makes out his cheque to the Receiver General of Canada, he finds that he also must pay an increase in tax for the old age pension fund. There are other taxes also such as sales tax which I will just mention in passing, and the increase in excise taxes. But when we take all of these taxes together, and take into consideration the 7 per cent increase in the gross national product, we do not go halfway in covering our deficit. I think the taxpayers of this country look to the future with foreboding. I think they feel that a better way in which to increase income taxes 
is to have a fiscal policy that would provide more people and more corporations paying these taxes.
I was looking over the corporation tax and I think this year it is up to the highest point in any peacetime year. In Ontario and in Quebec they are paying combined taxes-I mean by that the income tax plus the contributions to old age pensions-of 52 per cent. The other corporation taxes are very high, particularly when you add other provincial taxes and municipal taxes. Every tax adds to the cost of production. We know that our cost of production here in Canada is extremely high. We are having a hard time now to maintain our position in the highly competitive markets of the world. Representations have been made to Ottawa by manufacturers who say that they cannot compete in our own domestic market with foreign producers.
I have said before-and I will just refer to it here again-that the climate in Canada has not been good for United States capital to come in. It is really not good for our own corporations because of this increase in income tax. Our corporations in this country have already been heavily taxed and we are in the process of adding another $80 million a year to their costs by the fact that they are obliged to pay, along with their employees, for seasonal unemployment. I should think that the minister ought to know that the more industry we get in this country and the more people we get working, the more income taxes we shall collect. He should realize that the unemployment will then be taken up, more people will be working and we shall be able to tax more people instead of the fewer that we are taxing at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, there is just one aspect of this bill about which I should like to speak briefly, namely the change in the provision for deduction of hospital expenses. This is a principle with which many of us, I know, cannot agree. In the province of Ontario we are still obliged to pay the premiums which we paid before the new hospitalization plan came into effect. These premiums are not deductible from taxable income. They are paid out of net income but still the hospital bills are not going to be deductible from taxable income as they have been in the past.
This principle of allowing expenses in excess of a certain percentage of income is well established and has worked well because it alleviates much of the hardship which accrues when people undergo extensive illness personally or in their families. I know of many cases where the financial circumstances in the family have been such that without

the taxation relief granted they would have had to undergo severe and serious financial dislocation. As you know, we reduced the ceiling once or twice. There was considerable pressure in this house in years gone by to reduce it even further.
It was always stated that certain medical expenses were incidental to all people and that it would be administratively difficult to allow deductions for all medical expenses, and I think most people will agree with that. The expenses over and above a certain percentage of income are extraordinary expenses and certainly an exception can and should be made in those circumstances. Now this change has been made, part of the exemption which previously existed has been taken away and it is in fact, Mr. Speaker, just another form of taxation.
Surely the government did not have to squeeze the last drop out of the suffering of people who undergo lengthy and serious illness in order to increase its tax revenues. The minister in his budget speech indicated that in a full year some $9 million would be recovered by the federal treasury. This is a considerable amount of money, but I am positive that that amount of money in the hands of people who have suffered because of serious illness would do far more for Canadians generally than it would in the consolidated revenue fund.
It is therefore with regret, Mr. Speaker, that we have to consider a bill which contains this provision. I hope that the minister will give this matter some consideration between now and the time the next budget is brought down, and if he still occupies his present position at that time I hope that he will see fit to reverse himself.

Mr. Chairman, I address myself to clause 2 only because I find it extremely difficult to understand this complicated formula which by statute law is to me a little unique. There are set up five sections which do not state law but which state mathematics. You have for instance:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman is much too modest in disclaiming ability to understand this section. There are lots of provisions in the Income Tax Act which are much more lengthy and involved than this one.
So far as the mathematical formula is concerned, it is not part of the statute. It is here as one of the notes on the bill to give an illustration of the way in which the subclauses which are part of clause 2 of the bill will operate.
I think the hon. member is aware of the situation out of which this section has emerged. Group insurance policies which are provided, let us say, by an employer for an employee are exempt from income tax. In making use of that exemption we have found that a number of persons, let us say senior executives, have had very substantial policies written on their lives, and these enjoy an exemption which I am sure parliament did not intend in such large amounts. For instance, just because an executive happens to control a corporation, is it any good reason why he should enjoy the benefit of payment of premiums on a policy of, let us say, $100,000 on his life, tax free?

May I ask the minister if this is beyond the other sections of the bill

Income Tax Act
with respect to group policies? This is a possibility with a controlled company; is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I am speaking about group policies. These are commonly known, I believe, as jumbo policies, and they exist in many cases where there is no general provision assuring equality of treatment or even proportionate treatment on the part of employees of the company concerned. Therefore it seemed to us that there should be some limitation placed upon the exemption now enjoyed. That is why we brought forward the proposal that premiums paid on these policies should be exempt in the case of any person up to $25,000 of life insurance, but as to the excess of the insurance over $25,000, whatever premium is paid on behalf of the individual should be regarded as income received by him and he should be taxable upon it. Otherwise, it would be relatively simple for a senior executive to take a substantial portion of his remuneration not in the form of salary but in the form of an extraordinarily large insurance policy upon which premiums would be paid on his behalf. That is the background out of which this proposal has come to the committee.
This clause deals-and deals in a straight forward way, I think-with the person who has been enjoying the benefit of a policy of more than $25,000, or who will in future be enjoying the benefit of such a policy under one of the group insurance plans. How are you going to tax such a person in respect of the premium on the excess over $25,000? That is the situation with which this clause deals. One could go about it in two ways, broadly speaking. One could say: we will regard as income in the hands of such a man the premium which he would pay at his age on that particular policy according to its amount and its provisions. But that might not be fair, because the man might be advanced in age; he might, indeed, have reached a point where insurance premiums are very heavy. He might even have passed the point where he can obtain insurance on an individual policy. What we have done, therefore, is, in effect, to work out an average so that what such a man will have to pay is the average premium on the whole group under the group plan. That is the essence, briefly, of this clause. It is well understood, I can assure the hon. gentleman, by the insurance companies. They understand what this means, and the way in which the plan works out.

May I ask whether an
estimate has been made as to the additional revenue which is expected to flow to the government from this source?
[Hr. Benidickson.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. It was not possible to work out any such calculation at all precisely. This proposal is put forward in the interests of the fair and equal treatment of taxpayers and to put an end to a situation in which some taxpayers were enjoying what was regarded as an unfair advantage under an existing exemption.

I realize the difficulty experienced in such legislation as this, but it seems to me that there is discrimination not only between people in different provinces but also between people in the same province. For instance, in Ontario it is optional whether people contribute to hospital insurance or not. I think the person who takes the insurance is penalized because his hospital bill is not deductible for income tax purposes. But if a person takes out an insurance policy which pays for hospitalization, those payments are deductible. Then, in connection with the provinces, if a person resides in a participating province there will be practically no hospital bills eligible for deduction, whereas in a province which does not participate every bill will be eligible for deduction. Thus I think there is a good deal of discrimination in this particicular clause between, as I said before, individuals in a province such as Ontario and persons in non-participating provinces.

I think with regard to this particular proposed change the minister has made a very grave mistake. Reference has been made to the increased amount of revenue, but in the minds of the people-[DOT] their imaginations in this respect stimulated very largely by some of the good speeches made by the hon. gentleman on this subject when he was sitting in the opposition to the effect that this was a proper tax deduction -the government's present intentions are causing great consternation. I just want to read a short excerpt from a letter I received on this point which, I think, will impress the minister. The letter comes from the international association of machinists and it says:
We protest the noncontinuance of hospitalization payments as paid by the provincial hospitalization plan as an income tax deduction.
I raised this matter on two or three other occasions in the debate which was open to all of us. Someone said-I think it was tonight-that the tax saving would amount to $9 million. That may be so, but I think the principle which existed in the past is

still valid. He also points out that inasmuch as the important province of Quebec is not participating in this hospitalization scheme the taxpayer had an opportunity of having a recognized insurance agency, the Blue Cross or whatever it may be, as his authorized agent for the purpose of presenting accounts to the Minister of National Revenue when income tax time comes around as a proper deduction if the over-all expenditure is more than 3 per cent of taxable income. Would the minister comment on the discriminatory aspects of this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were commented on fully in the discussion which took place in this house on May 4. The minister just repeats and repeats that there is no discrimination. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I have outlined the basis of deduction under this law. Income Tax Act
I put the fundamental question, as I have on previous occasions. The federal government is paying half of the cost of all hospitalization and diagnostic services provided by this act. It is costing the federal treasury this year $160 million in those provinces which have subscribed.
Fifty per cent of the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It averages 50 per cent across the dominion. In some provinces the federal share is more than 50 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I want to do what I do not often do, namely compliment the minister on this change. I think it does make it possible for a little greater freedom in transferring from one employment to another. The minister explained this on the resolution stage.

speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman.

On clause 13-Associated corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I would like to make a comment on clause 13, as it may be of interest. This provision which we are making by way of continuing the benefits enjoyed by the corporation which has an income of less than $25,000 is, of course, subject to certain terms in the act. I draw attention particularly to the provisions of section 39, subsection 4 of the act. I may say that my attention has been drawn to certain problems connected with this provision. It sets forth rules which are followed in determining whether or not corporations are associated with one another through ownership of shares. In particular, a corporation is not regarded as being associated with another corporation unless 70 per cent of its shares are owned by the other. This latter percentage was inserted in the act several years ago by an amendment. It was intended to relieve corporate taxpayers of certain difficulties with which they were being confronted. As a result, however, there are indications that it may be becoming too easy under this provision to divide a corporation into a number of smaller components, each of which qualifies for the lower rate of tax on its first $25,000 of income.
Although no conclusion has been reached as yet on this matter, I should like to inform the committee that consideration is being

Income Tax Act
given to the possible necessity of introducing in the future some further change in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I move:
That Bill C-48, An act to amend the Income Tax Act, be amended by striking out lines 25 to 34 on page 11 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
'unless,
(a)	in the case of a corporation that had a taxation year ending before 1959, the corporation was during its last taxation year ending before 1959 and each subsequent taxation year, if any, previous to the particular taxation year a foreign business corporation,
(b)	in the case of a corporation incorporated on or before April 9, 1959 that did not have a taxation year ending before 1959, the corporation was during its first taxation year ending after 1958 and each subsequent year, if any previous to the particular taxation year a foreign business corporation, or
(c)	in the case of a corporation that had a taxation year ending on or before April 9. 1959, the corporation was during its taxation year in which that date occurred and each subsequent taxation year, if any, previous to the particular taxation year a foreign business corporation, and had during that part of its taxation year in which that date occurred that was before April 10, 1959 business operations that complied with one of the conditions contained in paragraph (c) of subsection (2).'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that the purpose of the amendment is to enlarge the conditions under which corporations can qualify as foreign business corporations under this provision.

Mr. Chairman, the minister will recollect the debate we had at the resolution stage. It was only because of a little better assistance from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that we got from the minister some indication of why the administration felt that a change was necessary here. I am not going to deal further with it. I realize in effect we have a pause. The administration indicates that in the meantime they are giving consideration to all the aspects connected with this. I just want to say, because this seems to be the best opportunity of saying it-and I am not scolding-that in every possible way I think the minister should, in introducing a bill of this kind which imposes a tax upon people, see to it that it is presented to the house at a time when it will get the widest possible publicity
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).1
among the trade and financial papers and people who are expert in these matters. I mentioned this to the minister before, I think. As it happens, there was a delay in presenting this bill. I think it only came before the house for first reading on Wednesday last, and the bill amending the Excise Tax Act on the same day. A humble member was not able to get a copy of the bill until Thursday. I simply want to say to the minister that to my mind it is important in a democracy that the widest possible advance notice be given of amendments such as he is now proposing, resulting from presentations that have been made to him.
The minister and the administration should seek to have their views in this respect put in bill form at a time sufficiently in advance of debate in the house to ensure that people from coast to coast in our widespread country will have the opportunity to know the implications. I must also confess that it is a great advantage to humble people in the opposition to receive comments from these people.
But this was not possible in one or two respects and irrespective of whether or not the minister is moving on I suggest to him but more particularly to the officials that they should always see to it that amendments involving changes that are not in the resolutions and the bills are announced to the public before the House of Commons is asked to deal with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think we have tried to do that. This is a shorter bill than usual in the case of the amendments to the Income Tax Act. The bill follows the provisions of the resolutions which were before the house and the country for three and a half weeks prior to being adopted in committee of ways and means, and six days have now passed since the bill was introduced and given first reading. I think the bill has had wide publicity. We had the benefit of the usual discussion between officials of the department and the representatives of the Canadian tax foundation. They were here last week for detailed discussion which, as the hon. member knows, is customary, and following that detailed discussion Mr. Perry, the director of the tax foundation, intimated to me that they had no submissions to make on the bill.
So far as the amendment now introduced is concerned, it is one which widens the provisions of the bill and to that extent it can be regarded as a relieving section.

I simply want to say that the minister and his officials should be well aware that our financial papers usually come out on Wednesday or Thursday. They have

a wide circulation and if a bill is presented to the house on Thursday, prior to the time that these national papers can give it some comment, there is a possibility, particularly when there are amendments and changes not announced at budget time, that the public as a whole have not had a proper opportunity to present their views to their members of parliament.
I should like to ask the minister my usual question with respect to this amendment. No amendment was indicated at the resolution stage or when the bill was presented a little late, as I say, last Wednesday. Have there been any protests by anybody in the industry who has seen the purport of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Several submissions were received with respect to the extent and terms of the original proposal.
And this is the result.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amendment which I introduced in the committee was commended by those who had made the original submissions and this further amendment was suggested by one of them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 20-Amount of premium deductible.

I should like to ask the
minister a question largely prompted by a combination of my dullwittedness and suspicious nature. In subclause 2 of clause 20 the amending words are:
-or in the case of a taxpayer who is an employee of a life insurance corporation and is a beneficiary, contingently or otherwise, under a registered pension plan instituted or established by the corporation.
The explanation of the amendment on the opposite page reads as follows:
This amendment adds the underlined words to make it clear that employees of life insurance corporations, who are members of a registered pension plan established by such corporation for their employees, are subject to the limitations on the amount they may deduct as premiums under a registered retirement savings plan in the same manner as other taxpayers who are members of employee pension plans. The present wording of the paragraph being amended does not cover employees of life Insurance corporations because these corporations have special rules for computing their taxable income.
Was this amendment found necessary because of some discovery as to the method of computing income tax of life insurance companies on the part of the minister's officials, and can he explain what is meant by the words "these corporations have special rules for computing their taxable income?"
Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Questions were
asked as to whether the persons here referred to were in fact so bound. That is what gave rise to a consideration of this question. I might say broadly in reply to the hon. gentleman that taxpayers who are members of registered pension plans may also deduct premiums paid under registered retirement savings plans but the combined total of the contributions into the two kinds of plans may not exceed 10 per cent of income or $1,500 per year. Taxpayers who are not members of registered pension plans may deduct premiums not exceeding 10 per cent of income up to a maximum $2,500 per year.
This amendment makes it clear that life insurance employees who are members of registered pension plans are subject to the $1,500 maximum the same as other employees who are members of such plans. The purpose of the bill is to achieve equality of treatment. The limit on the amount deductible is lower for those who are members of registered pension plans because, in addition to deducting their own contributions, they also exclude from income during their working years amounts paid into the registered pension plan on their behalf by their employer.
Was the amendment occasioned by a misunderstanding on the part of some people filing income tax returns or some irregularities on the part of employees of these companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no discovery in that sense. No irregularity was discovered. It was a matter of a normal review and an attempt to assure equality.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I indicate to the house leader that Bill No. C-49 which he intends to take on Thursday was just handed to us a few moments ago; as a matter of fact it was handed to us when the evening session had begun. This is an extremely important bill. We have co-operated with the government in getting the resolution through in excellent time, I believe. But here we are handed a bill which has 101 clauses extending over 28 pages. I do not think it is equitable on the part of the government to ask the opposition, on this short notice, to be ready to discuss second reading of a bill of this importance. I wonder whether the house leader would not give consideration to putting this bill over, as surely must have been the intention of all the members of the house, for discussion on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I always try to meet the wishes of the opposition but in this case I am afraid I cannot do so. There is a great urgency to get this measure through on the part of the people of western Canada. There comes times when we just cannot give the extra time that is requested. As the hon. member has mentioned, we arranged to distribute the bill this afternoon. There will be a day tomorrow and until 3.30 p.m. approximately on Thursday. I am sorry but I cannot accede to the wishes of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My submission is that on 24 hours' notice we cannot possibly give to this bill the attention that it requires and that I am sure parliament should give. The point

I am making is this. While it might be urgent to get this measure through, surely it was just as urgent to bring it on earlier. If we had had it brought on earlier I am sure we would have had the requisite amount of time in which to consider it. It seems to me that this is taking an unfair advantage of the members of the opposition in asking them to deal with a matter of this importance, with the time that is being given at the moment.
It was mentioned in the speech from the throne.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is really an outrageous way in which to treat the House of Commons. Hon. gentlemen opposite used to talk about a deadline.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Unless the minister is prepared to change his position, there is no point in pursuing the matter further. It being ten o'clock-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think we have been rather fair on this side of the house tonight. We have allowed the excise tax bill and the income tax bill to go through. We have sat after ten o'clock. It seems to me that this matter is one of extreme importance. I repeat that we are going to consider carefully the attitude which we shall have to take on this bill in view of the position taken by the leader of the house. I repeat that the position he has taken is not fair to us on this side of the house. This is the first time that I have made this protest on any of the matters that have been brought to the attention of the house for the next day's business. I am sure the leader of the house will bear me out when I say this. This is the first time in my recollection that I have risen, on an occasion such as this, to protest the inadequacy of the time given us for consideration of a bill of this importance. I gave the information which concerns this matter to the leader of our party and he thinks it just unconscionable that we should be asked, with barely 24 hours' notice, to deal with this bill. I ask the leader of the house whether in fairness he will not reconsider his position and allow us to deal with it over the week end so that we can discuss it intelligently on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member has been extremely co-operative and I appreciate his actions throughout. However, in this case I regret that I cannot accede to his suggestion.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that I think he is under-rating his intelligence.

speechtext: It being ten minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
